newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Vietnam coffee stagnates on a lack of liquidity.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam coffee stagnates on a lack of liquidity.

text.p: Vietnam coffee prices were stagnant this week on a lack of liquidity caused by exports held up at congested ports and the large quantity of already contracted sales, Southeast Asian traders said on Wednesday.
Indonesian robusta prices were also seen steady to a touch easier, with the current crop shaping up very well and harvesting expected to get underway in March or April.
Traders said Vietnam's coffee exports are "running at full capacity" ahead of the Chinese Lunar New Year festivities in early February.
Ho Chi Minh port remains heavily congested and there are no signs that the logjam will ease until March, traders said.

"Most of these cargoes have already been sold earlier and currently the customers are taking deliveries," said one trader. Traders said as most deals had been concluded earlier, prices hardly moved from last week due to lack of liquidity.
Vietnam's benchmark Grade 2, 8.0 percent black and broken was quoted at between $950-$1,050 a tonne FOB Saigon.

"Vietnam would have sold about 50-60 percent of its crop already and I do not expect the congestion to ease until March," the trader said. He said for the remaining 40 percent of the crop, Vietnam would probably spread the sales out over the balance of the year.
But another trader said Vietnamese firms are more likely to "try to sell as much as they can before prices start to fall."

Another added that Vietnam had undersold by around 25,000 tonnes last December and is likely to "make up for the lost sales" in its current crop. "This would add to the volume they were likely to sell in early February" he said.

Traders had a mixed view on Indonesian robusta coffee prices. One trader said prices had eased slightly to around $1,150 a tonne FOB Panjang, but others said prices were largely unchanged at between $1,250-$1,300 a tonne.
"Indonesia is likely to export around six to seven and a half million bags this crop and harvesting would start in March or April. So far, their crops looks good," he said.
Thailand's agricultural ministry has revised its coffee output forecast down to 79,027 tonnes from 81,731 tonnes projected earlier.
Traders said sales of African coffee have already started and more Brazilian coffee is likely to be exported this year estimated at 20 million 60-kg bags.
"These additional crops are likely place pressure on prices in the near term," said a trader.
But traders generally said coffee futures could still build on current bullish momentum, although a widening differential between the London and New York markets may cause the trend to falter.
"There is still room for prices to move up as the undertone remains strong with the recent rally seen in New York and London" said a trader in Singapore.
"But when the price differential between New York and London gets wide enough, to around $1.00 per pound, we may see the price trend reversing," he said.
A total of 206 tonnes were traded on Tuesday on the Singapore Commodity Exchange's (SICOM) March and May coffee contracts. The settlement prices were $1,346 and $1,326 a tonne respectively.
